name: Marco Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, unions, AI companies, parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a workday sound like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I came to paid trombone after years selling rail tickets. I play a junior chair in a theatre pit, record short cues and teach two beginners under a paid senior brass teacher. I still get a slide position wrong when I rush, but the thrill is hitting the entrance with the cast.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What steadies life outside the pit?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, my partner works at a hardware shop, and our grown children are on their own. We have a mortgage and eight months of expenses saved, and the theatre pays well for my junior part; plenty of venues are close enough to reach by train. I use AI now and then to draft a rehearsal calendar, then check every time with the stage manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the cast that a faster timetable is welcome if paid pit and rehearsal hours stay visible. I would still check the call with the stage manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The theatre run and two supervised pupils pay steadily, and my partner’s shop hours are regular. Eight months saved gives us room if a show closes between seasons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep paid pit calls, cue recordings and two supervised pupils, and ask for the next run’s rehearsal fees in writing. In a plateau’s first year I would request an actual pension estimate before choosing a retirement date and save one fifth of cleared extra cue fees after mortgage, food and train fares toward twelve months of bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our bills in this picture. A written call sheet beats guessing whether the Tuesday rehearsal pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the senior teacher stay in those lessons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the music school pays her to supervise while I teach basics. I am still learning, and I do not promise advanced brass lessons alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the pension estimate decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing by itself. My partner and I would put the real figure beside our bills before setting any date.

I would check **theatre calls** with the stage manager.
think: Our **eight-month reserve** covers an ordinary gap between shows.
I need an **actual pension estimate** before choosing a retirement date.
do: Keep **pit and pupils** with paid recordings, supervision and written rehearsal fees.
Request **pension estimate**; save fifth of cleared extra cue fees after bills toward twelve months.
feel: I feel **calm** about current income and mortgage bills.

fieldNote: His **junior teaching** remains under a senior brass teacher paid by the school.
The **eight-month reserve** and well-paid current theatre run support a calm plateau despite their mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the theatre which short cue recordings still use paid players. I would tell beginners that a safe trombone and an experienced teacher matter more than a clever poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect fewer paid cue recordings and perhaps fewer preparation calls. That is a real part of my pay, although eight months saved lets us check alternatives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the paid pit and supervised pupils and ask for written cue and rehearsal rates. If two monthly cue calls disappear, I would offer a separate beginner brass class only after the room booking and hire charge are agreed in writing before deposits; six paid deposits must cover my teaching/preparation, a paid senior teacher, room hire, safe instrument hire and train fares; I would replace an unsafe trombone or defer and refund the whole group if six safe paid places cannot remain, and renew during disruption only when six places cover every wage and cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about cue fees shrinking. I will not make the senior teacher donate her time to keep a class alive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a rented trombone has a sticking slide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would get a safe replacement before the class starts. If I cannot keep six safe paid places, I would defer and refund the whole group, not count that instrument as a seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you take deposits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After the hall confirms the room in writing. I will not take money for a date I cannot deliver.

I would tell families **safe instruments** and an experienced teacher matter.
think: I expect **recording and preparation fees** to fall.
The **eight-month reserve** lets us test demand without unpaid teaching.
do: Keep **paid pit and pupils** while requesting written cue and rehearsal rates.
Start **brass class** after two lost cues; agree written room/hire before deposits; six fees cover own teaching/prep, senior wage, room, instruments/trains.
Replace **unsafe trombone** or defer/refund whole group below six safe places; renew only when six places pay all wages/costs, including room.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a plausible loss of cue fees.
S1.quote: I will not make the senior teacher donate her time to keep a class alive.
fieldNote: Six **safe paid places** must cover written room hire, his teaching/prep, senior wage, safe instruments and train travel.
A failed **instrument replacement** means deferral and refund of the whole group below the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the pit that 2028 thinking AGI could plan and make cue recordings before robot trombonists around 2031. I would ask for paid rehearsals on paper now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect cue work to stop and one theatre rehearsal day to be cut in 2028. That would take a noticeable piece of my pay, even though our savings buy time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I would get written pit dates and keep the two supervised pupils. In the first year after 2028, if cues end and a rehearsal day goes, I would apply for a posted paid theatre-front-desk role only if my secondary schooling and rail-ticket experience qualify, its written net pay after train fares replaces lost music fees and the route works; I would keep pit and pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the fast cut, not unable to act. Nearby venues may hire, but each needs an actual paid opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your ticketing years count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put them on an application, but the posted requirements decide. A box-office desk is familiar work, not an automatic job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about robot players?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The card puts capable trombone robots around 2031. Planning and cue prices could change in 2028, so I would check the contract first.

I would ask for **written paid rehearsals** now.
think: I expect **cue and rehearsal pay** to fall.
Our **eight-month reserve** gives time to seek real paid work.
do: Keep **pit and supervised pupils** with written dates before 2028 and until signed replacement offer.
Seek **posted theatre desk role** after 2028 cue/rehearsal loss, requiring qualifying schooling/ticketing, written replacement net after trains and workable route.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a noticeable cut to my own fees.
S2.quote: A box-office desk is familiar work, not an automatic job.
fieldNote: The **2028 risk** reaches planning and recorded cues before robot pit playing.
The **desk option** requires a posted paid opening, accepted schooling and ticketing experience, plus written replacement net pay.

steps.text: Keep paid pit and supervised pupils; request written dates before 2028 until signed offer
Seek posted theatre desk role after cue/rehearsal loss; schooling/ticketing qualify, written replacement net after trains, route

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years lets us check what the theatre will still pay for live players. Thinking AGI arrives around 2031 and robot trombonists around 2034 in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cue recordings may fade before the pit does. I could use the time to see whether a theatre desk qualification is worth taking, but I will not pay for a course no employer recognises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep paid pit and supervised pupils and look at actual posted theatre-front-desk roles. If cues end and a rehearsal day is cut, I would take any required booking-system certificate only after a funded course place on paid time is confirmed, the employer says it recognises that certificate and my secondary schooling and ticketing experience meet the role; in the first year after 2031 I would move only on a signed written net offer after train fares replacing lost music pay and workable transport, keeping current work until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about cue income over the next few years. Five years is enough time to check a course and an offer, not a reason to leave a paid pit chair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would pay during the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The employer would have to fund the course and protect my paid hours while I attend. If there is no accepted place and paid time, I would keep playing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the theatre wants a different certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check its posting before enrolling. A certificate that the actual employer will not recognise is paper I cannot use.

I would explain **2031 thinking AGI** and robot trombonists around 2034.

feel: I feel **anxious** about recording losses but able to check actual options.
S3.quote: A certificate that the actual employer will not recognise is paper I cannot use.
fieldNote: The **course gate** requires an actual funded place, paid time and qualification recognition by a posted employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that thinking AGI around 2036 and robot trombonists around 2039 are different dates. I would still ask what a theatre rehearsal pays now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may prefer fewer evening shows, but I have no retirement date until I see an actual pension estimate. Eight months saved and the current pit run keep the next few years steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep paid pit and supervised pupils, request my actual pension estimate and save one fifth of cleared extra brass-class surplus after my teaching and preparation, senior teacher, room hire, safe instruments, trains, mortgage and food toward twelve months. Over the decade I would run the separate class only after written room booking and hire charge are agreed before deposits; six deposits must cover all those wages and costs, replacing unsafe instruments or deferring and refunding the whole group below six safe places; in the first year after 2036 I would renew only on the same full paid floor and keep pit work that still pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the far end of cue work. The present run and reserve cover our near-term bills. A long calendar does not guarantee a paid class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy six trombones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would hire safe ones against six paid places and leave the reserve for bills. A broken instrument gets replaced or the whole group is deferred and refunded below the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire when the pension figure arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My partner and I would compare the actual estimate with bills and health. A statement is information, not a command to stop playing.

Replace **unsafe instrument** or defer/refund whole group below six safe places; renew after 2036 only with every wage/cost, including room.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because cues and a rehearsal day could go before I have another wage. Written theatre dates, a real qualifying desk vacancy and a net offer after train fares would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the senior teacher before you call a beginner brass class profitable. My trombone still needs correction, and the senior teacher’s watchful hour is a real wage.

headlineQuote: My trombone still needs correction, and the senior teacher’s watchful hour is a real wage.
portrait: Marco is a **junior trombonist** still learning after rail-ticket work, with secondary schooling and strong theatre pay.
He has **eight months saved**, a hardware-shop partner, grown children and a mortgage.
He uses **AI occasionally** for draft schedules, checking them with the stage manager.
His **separate brass class** needs paid senior supervision, a written room and six safe paid places.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could cut cues and a rehearsal day before replacement wages arrive.
whatWouldHelp: He needs **written theatre dates**, an actual qualifying desk vacancy and net wages after train fares.
